# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

National Health Interview Survey
 

About NHIS

For Everyone
June 18, 2026

What to know

  • NHIS is the National Health Interview Survey.
  • NHIS is a national survey that monitors the health of the U.S. population.
  • NHIS statistics provide insights into the health of people of different ages, sexes, races and ethnicities, geographic locations, and social and economic circumstances.

Overview

The National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) monitors the health of people across the country—the U.S. population—by collecting and analyzing data on a broad range of health topics. NHIS focuses on the health of U.S. children and adults.

CDC's National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) conducts NHIS. It is the nation's largest and oldest national health survey. NHIS began collecting data in 1957.

Each year, NHIS collects data from about 27,000 adults through confidential, face-to-face interviews throughout the year. Many of these adults also provide health information about children in their households.

NHIS collects data from civilians who don't live in institutions. Civilians are people not serving on active duty in the military. Institutionalized people live in places like correctional facilities, skilled-nursing homes, and mental (psychiatric) hospitals.

NCHS is exploring new ways for you to participate in NHIS. Some people may receive a paper questionnaire while others will receive an invitation to complete the survey online. Some people may receive both. Your participation matters no matter how you complete the survey. If you need assistance with the survey or have questions, please call the number on the letter you received or email nhis@census.gov.

Selected to participate in the survey?

Learn why you should take part in NHIS and what to expect.
Visit our participant website

What's collected

NHIS collects data through personal interviews. One adult household member provides information about their own health and the health of others in their households.

NHIS collects data about health topics like—

  • Illness and chronic conditions
  • Injuries and chronic pain
  • Health-related behaviors
  • Ability to perform daily activities (functioning) and disability
  • Healthcare access and use
  • Health insurance coverage
  • Preventive services to identify and prevent health problems

The U.S. Census Bureau employs and trains field staff to conduct these interviews. They follow procedures developed by NCHS experts. Field staff conduct most interviews in person. Sometimes they conduct follow-up interviews over the phone.

Did you know?

NHIS content is updated about every 15–20 years to reflect advances in survey methodology and coverage of health topics. In 2019, NHIS launched redesigned content and structure that differs from the earlier questionnaire design (1997–2018).

Data and documentation

NCHS publishes reports featuring expert analysis of NHIS data. Selected estimates also are available as part of our interactive data query systems that provide tables and charts.

In producing these resources, NHIS staff prioritize protecting participants' privacy.

Data files

NHIS public use data files are available to download in multiple formats. All potentially identifiable information has been removed to ensure the confidentiality of participants and their households.

NHIS restricted data files are available through the National Center for Health Statistics Research Data Center (RDC) for a fee. To access restricted NHIS data, researchers must submit requests in the Standard Application Process portal. The RDC provides instructions for preparing and submitting an application to access restricted data.

NHIS data also has been linked with data from other sources. This provides more robust datasets that can be used to analyze complex relationships between data from different sources. These linked datasets are available in the RDC.

Find data documentation for these datasets at Questionnaires, Datasets, and Documentation.

How the data are used

NCHS staff use NHIS data to produce official national health estimates. One of NHIS's key strengths is its ability to produce estimates for many subgroups of the U.S. population. NHIS can do this because it collects data from such a large group of people.

NHIS health statistics provide health information by—

  • Demographic characteristics, like age and marital status
  • Geographic location, like region and metro area size
  • Social and economic circumstances, like employment status and poverty level

These data help researchers, policymakers, and other data users better understand how health differs among these groups.

NHIS data drive policies and programs to improve health. NHIS results have helped track the health status of Americans, their access to health care, and the nation's progress toward achieving health goals.

Contact us

Email nhis@cdc.gov with any questions about the National Health Interview Survey.

	<item>
		<title>Introducing: Variable-Based Sample Selection for IPUMS International</title>
		<link>https://blog.popdata.org/international-variable-based-sample-selection/</link>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[mpcblog]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Thu, 01 Oct 2026 20:05:27 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Data]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[IPUMS International]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://blog.popdata.org/?p=4227</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[When you’re building an IPUMS International extract, you almost always have a central topic or question in mind: How is children’s educational attainment influenced by their parents’ education levels? How have migration patterns in Latin America changed in the past few decades? How do age and disability status interact to influence employment?


In other words, you almost always know the main variables you want in your extract. To study education, you’ll need EDATTAIN. To study lifetime international migration, you’ll need BPLCOUNTRY. To study disability and employment, you’ll need DISABLED and EMPSTAT.

Wouldn’t it be great if there was a magic wand that could add all the samples with your variable(s) of interest to your extract with just a flick of the wrist?

If you’re nodding your head in agreement right now, we think you’ll love our new feature: variable based sample selection! It doesn’t involve a wand, but it is a magical way to select samples based on the variables you need.]]></description>
		
		
		
			</item>
		<item>
		<title>Continuity and Change in the 2025 NHIS Data</title>
		<link>https://blog.popdata.org/continuity-change-in-2025-nhis-data/</link>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[mpcblog]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Tue, 15 Sep 2026 15:22:14 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Data]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[IPUMS Health Surveys]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://blog.popdata.org/?p=4242</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[Collected annually since 1957, the National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) is the longest running nationally-representative health survey in the world. The NHIS questionnaire and data collection approaches have changed considerably over time, both to better capture emerging public health topics as well as to adapt the study design, questionnaire, and data collection operations to maintain a high-quality data product. The objective of this blog post is understanding the factors that contribute to year-to-year change in variables available from the NHIS with a particular focus on the 2025 NHIS data.]]></description>
		
		
		
			</item>
		<item>
		<title>Comparing Census Bureau and IPUMS USA Inflation Adjustments to American Community Survey Income Variables</title>
		<link>https://blog.popdata.org/comparing-census-bureau-and-ipums-usa-inflation-adjustments-to-american-community-survey-income-variables/</link>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[mpcblog]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Tue, 18 Aug 2026 20:23:20 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Data]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[IPUMS USA]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://blog.popdata.org/?p=4207</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[Researchers working with variables that report income must account for the changing value of a dollar across time. IPUMS USA, and other IPUMS data collections, include resources that streamline the process of adjusting monetary variables into constant dollars to facilitate comparison. These tools are very useful for researchers who are initiating research projects and exclusively using IPUMS data; however, these tools can make it difficult to directly compare, for example, IPUMS and the original U.S. Census Bureau versions of public use microdata sample (PUMS) data. This blog post provides an overview of how the Census Bureau reports income values in the American Community Survey (ACS) PUMS data, the adjustment factors provided by the Census Bureau, and how those map onto variables and ACS microdata extracts from IPUMS USA.]]></description>
		
		
		
			</item>
		<item>
		<title>IPUMS Time Use Leadership Receives Ellen Galinsky Generative Researcher Award</title>
		<link>https://blog.popdata.org/ipums-time-use-leadership-award/</link>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[mpcblog]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Thu, 16 Jul 2026 20:01:34 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Featured]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[IPUMS Time Use]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://blog.popdata.org/?p=4196</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[Since 1993, IPUMS has worked to preserve and harmonize the population data and make them freely accessible to researchers. This includes time diary data from the American Time Use Survey (ATUS) as well as international and historical time diary data. Last month, Drs. Sarah Flood and Liana Sayer, co-PIs of IPUMS Time Use, along with their long-time collaborator Dr. Melissa Milkie, received the Ellen Galinsky Generative Researcher Award, presented by the Work and Family Researchers Network.

The award recognizes work-family researchers who have contributed breakthrough thinking to the work-family field via theory, measures, and/or data sets that led to expansive application, innovation, and diffusion, including the sharing of research opportunities in the spirit of open science. The award committee highlighted Flood’s foundational contributions to public data infrastructure and long history of demystifying complex time diary data, as well as Sayer’s innovative scholarship on gender and social class inequalities in time use over the life course.]]></description>
		
		
		
			</item>
		<item>
		<title>Family Interrelationships Variables in IPUMS MEPS</title>
		<link>https://blog.popdata.org/family-interrelationships-variables-in-ipums-meps/</link>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[mpcblog]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Wed, 01 Jul 2026 19:45:29 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Data]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[IPUMS Health Surveys]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[IPUMS MEPS]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://blog.popdata.org/?p=4186</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[Researchers interested in families and health may add a new tool to their toolkit: IPUMS family interrelationship variables are now available in IPUMS MEPS! Also known as family pointers, these variables increase reproducibility, flexibility and ease of use when analyzing family units and relationships within households – whether users are interested in isolating simple parent-child dyads or in assembling more complex family units potentially involving multigenerational and multifamily arrangements.

IPUMS has pioneered the development of family pointers, and these variables have since been added to most of our data collection projects. Their recent addition to IPUMS MEPS presents exciting opportunities owing to the unique richness of the MEPS data, which includes the possibility to eventually expand these pointers to a panel format.]]></description>
		
		
		
			</item>
		<item>
		<title>Does 1 + 2 = 8? Automating QA/QC for Tabular Data</title>
		<link>https://blog.popdata.org/automating-qa-qc-for-tabular-data/</link>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[mpcblog]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Thu, 21 May 2026 14:23:35 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Data]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[IHGIS]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://blog.popdata.org/?p=4173</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[The problem with OCR and numbers

To extract data tables from census reports only available as print documents, IPUMS IHGIS uses optical character recognition (OCR) software to automate the conversion of scanned images into digital representations of letters and numbers. OCR software has made great strides in accuracy for textual information by using dictionaries of known words to interpret uncertain letters. However, dictionaries do not help in distinguishing uncertain numerical digits. While a dictionary can suggest that the third character in “wh_t” should be an ‘a’ and not an ‘o’, there is no simple way to tell whether the third digit in “45_” should be a 3 or an 8. To ensure that IHGIS data are accurate, we must have confidence that each number has been recognized correctly and matches the number in the source document.

To address this gap, we developed an R package that leverages IHGIS structured metadata to identify logical relationships between cell counts and row/column totals and determine where cells don’t add up as expected. Often, a given cell participates in multiple relationships, which allows the package to use patterns among discrepancies to pinpoint and correct errors. The package can automatically identify and correct up to 95% of error cells, depending on the structure of relationships.]]></description>
		
		
		
			</item>
		<item>
		<title>IPUMS Announces 2025 Research Award Recipients</title>
		<link>https://blog.popdata.org/2025-research-award/</link>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[mpcblog]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Wed, 13 May 2026 20:03:57 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Administration]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Dissemination and Outreach]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Featured]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://blog.popdata.org/?p=4160</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[IPUMS is excited to announce the winners of its annual IPUMS Research Awards. These awards honor both published research and nominated graduate student papers from 2025 that use IPUMS data to advance or deepen our understanding of social and demographic processes. The 2025 competition awarded prizes for both published and graduate student research in eight categories, each associated with specific IPUMS data collections: IPUMS USA, IPUMS CPS, IPUMS International, IPUMS Health Surveys, IPUMS Spatial, IPUMS Global Health, IPUMS Time Use, and IPUMS Excellence in Research. Over 2,200 publications based on IPUMS data appeared in journals, magazines, and newspapers worldwide last year. From these publications and from nominated graduate student papers, the award committees selected the 2025 honorees.]]></description>
		
		
		
			</item>
		<item>
		<title>IPUMS DHS Goes Global</title>
		<link>https://blog.popdata.org/ipums-dhs-goes-global/</link>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[mpcblog]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Mon, 04 May 2026 16:11:25 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Data]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[IPUMS DHS]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://blog.popdata.org/?p=4147</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[IPUMS DHS now includes integrated variables for 84 counties (up from 51) and nearly 350 samples (up from 233), including new data from Latin America, Eastern Europe, Oceania, the Caribbean, and Central and East Asia. Providing DHS data in a form that facilitates micro-analyses across countries is one of IPUMS' greatest strengths, so researchers will be excited to learn that they can now do even more! Our latest data release expands the scope of IPUMS DHS beyond its initial coverage of Africa, the Middle East, and South Asia and adds the latest samples for 12 countries previously in the database. Figure 1 shows the full geographic scope of IPUMS DHS, as well as highlighting newly added countries and previously included countries with new samples.]]></description>
		
		
		
			</item>
		<item>
		<title>Adjust Monetary Values for IPUMS CPS</title>
		<link>https://blog.popdata.org/adjust-monetary-values-cps/</link>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[mpcblog]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Wed, 01 Apr 2026 15:01:24 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[IPUMS CPS]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://blog.popdata.org/?p=2979</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[We love to extend useful functionality across multiple IPUMS data collections, so we were delighted to extend the the Adjust Monetary Values (AMV) feature, which adjusts dollar values for inflation and was first developed for IPUMS USA, to IPUMS CPS. The initial release of the AMV feature in IPUMS CPS in 2023 provided adjustment for a limited number of variables. Late last year, we extended the feature to cover variables from the ASEC as well. This blog post provides a quick introduction to the AMV tool and step-by-step guidance for using the tool in IPUMS CPS.]]></description>
		
		
		
			</item>
		<item>
		<title>Linking children and adolescents to their mothers using IPUMS MICS</title>
		<link>https://blog.popdata.org/linking-children-adolescents-to-mothers-using-ipums-mics/</link>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[mpcblog]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Fri, 20 Mar 2026 17:09:24 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Data]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[IPUMS Global Health]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[IPUMS MICS]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://blog.popdata.org/?p=4041</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[IPUMS MICS offers hundreds of harmonized variables related to children's health and wellbeing that allow for rich and innovative research. From the IPUMS MICS website, users can browse variables and create custom data extracts within a selected unit of analysis. In order to conduct many analyses, however, users will want to combine and link datasets relating to different units of analysis available in MICS.

For example, to investigate how child characteristics are related to characteristics of their mother, users will need to download and link data between the Children 0-4 unit of analysis and the Women unit of analysis.

IPUMS MICS provides instructions for linking across units of analysis as a user note. This user note lists the variables available as linking keys for each unit of analysis, and is a general guide for linking across the units, such as linking household characteristics with individual person records.

In this blog post, we provide more detailed information on how to link children and adolescents to their mothers. Similar logic can be applied to fathers or other caregivers in the household. As IPUMS MICS requires Stata to conduct harmonization, we provide example code in Stata syntax.
]]></description>
		
		
		
			</item>

## 1. Identification and Publication

| Attribute | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Dataset title** | National Health Interview Survey (NHIS) |

A key operational detail often missed: while NCHS designs the survey and owns the data, **the U.S. Census Bureau conducts the fieldwork** — it employs and trains the interviewers, operating on behalf of NCHS under Title 13 U.S.C. §8(b). Interviews are typically initiated in person at respondents' homes, with follow-ups by telephone; in 2024, 53.2% of Sample Adult interviews were conducted at least partially by telephone.

## 2. Legal Authority and Mandate

The NHIS rests on a deep statutory foundation — an accumulation of public laws over more than 40 years:

- **National Health Survey Act of 1956 (P.L. 84-652, signed July 3, 1956)** — the originating authority. It called for "a continuing survey and special studies" to secure accurate and current statistical information on the amount, distribution, and effects of illness and disability in the United States and the services rendered for such conditions. Notably, it also explicitly mandated research into survey methods and techniques and authorized cooperation with other agencies.
- **Current codified authority: Section 306 of the Public Health Service Act (42 U.S.C. 242k)** — authorizes NCHS to collect national statistics on illness and disability, their economic impact, environmental and social health hazards, determinants of health, health resources, use and costs of health care, and family formation/dissolution. The Census Bureau confirms NHIS data collection is authorized under this section.
- **Health Services Research and Evaluation and Health Statistics Act of 1974 (P.L. 93-353)** — established NCHS in law and codified its mandate under Section 306.
- **Heart Disease, Cancer, Stroke, and Kidney Disease Amendments of 1970 (P.L. 91-515)** — established the **confidentiality provisions** for national health surveys that remain in force today (Section 308(d) of the PHS Act). These provisions make it unlawful to identify NHIS respondents and underpin all of NCHS's data-release practices.
- NCHS is one of the government's **thirteen principal statistical agencies**, giving NHIS the standing of an official federal statistical product (relevant to data quality standards, confidentiality law, and Statistical Policy Directives).

## 3. History

- **1953:** A subcommittee of the National Committee on Vital and Health Statistics recommends a permanent national health survey.
- **1956:** National Health Survey Act passed; funds appropriated the same month.
- **July 1957:** The survey (originally just "the U.S. National Health Survey") begins data collection.
- **1960:** NCHS is created by merging the National Health Survey program with the National Office of Vital Statistics; NCHS has conducted the survey since.
- **Content redesigns roughly every 10–20 years:** major questionnaire redesigns in 1997 (introducing the Family Core / Sample Adult / Sample Child structure) and **2019** (see below). Sample designs are redrawn after each decennial census (current design implemented 2016, with tweaks in 2018).
- **2019 redesign (the big one for data users):** the first structural overhaul in more than 20 years. The family questionnaire was eliminated; the survey now consists of three modules — Household Roster, Sample Adult interview, and Sample Child interview — with one randomly selected adult and one randomly selected child per household. Content was reorganized into Annual Core, **Rotating Core** (topics appearing every 2–3 years), Sponsored Content (paid for by other federal agencies, e.g., food security, cancer screening), and **Emerging Content** (e.g., opioid use in 2019, COVID-19 questions 2020–2022). Weighting was overhauled to use multilevel regression models with paradata to address nonresponse bias, calibrated to Census population projections and American Community Survey variables. **Consequence: estimates from 2019 forward are generally not comparable to 1997–2018 without care.**
- **Ongoing:** NCHS is currently planning a **2028 questionnaire redesign** to modernize data collection (including web/paper self-response modes), and has added **NHIS-Teen** (data about teens collected from teens themselves, added in 2021) and oversamples/supplements such as the **2014 Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander NHIS**.

## 4. Methodology (for the data scientist)

- **Design:** Stratified, multistage probability sample of households and noninstitutional group quarters. The U.S. is divided into 1,689 geographic areas (counties or groups), stratified partly by urban/rural density, with clusters of ~2,500 addresses sampled within strata; the 10 least populous states and D.C. get slightly oversampled clusters to ensure minimum state representation.
- **Sample sizes:** ~27,000–33,000 sample adults and ~8,000–9,000 sample children annually (target under the 2019 redesign: 27,000 adults and 9,000 children). Historically (pre-2019) the full household survey covered on the order of 100,000 persons in ~40,000–45,000 households per year.
- **Response rates:** A critical caveat. Final response rates have declined substantially: 2023 Sample Adult 47.0% / Sample Child 44.9%; 2024 Sample Adult 47.9% / Sample Child 45.8%. (Response rates were higher pre-pandemic and dipped sharply in 2020.) Analysts must use the provided weights (which include the paradata-informed nonresponse adjustments) and should report per the **PRICSSA** guidelines (Preferred Reporting Items for Complex Sample Survey Analysis) that NCHS publishes for each year.
- **Topics:** health status, chronic conditions, injuries and pain, functioning/disability, health behaviors (smoking, alcohol, physical activity), healthcare access and use, health insurance, preventive services, and demographics/socioeconomics.
- **The pre/post-2019 break:** after 2018 there is no more person-level data on all household members; family-level content (insurance for other members, some employment/earnings, country of birth, etc.) is collected only for the sample adult's/child's family.

## 5. Data Products, Access, and Preservation (for the data librarian/preservationist)

**Public-use microdata:**
- Free, no registration required, downloadable from the NHIS documentation pages and NCHS's open FTP server (ftp.cdc.gov) — ASCII, CSV, and SAS files, with SAS/SPSS/Stata input statements. Historical files going back to 1963 are available.
- Imputed income files: because income/earnings nonresponse is high, NCHS releases **multiply imputed** family income, personal earnings, employment, and poverty-ratio files (five implicates per year, 1997–present).
- **Public-Use Linked Mortality Files:** NHIS respondents (1986–2018 survey years) linked to National Death Index death certificate records, with perturbed/synthetic dates and causes of death to protect confidentiality — these enable prospective mortality studies without restricted access.
- Annual releases of questionnaires, survey descriptions, variance-estimation guidance, and PRICSSA checklists accompany each year's files.

**Restricted data:**
- Restricted-use variables (including detailed geography/geocodes) and most linked datasets (Medicare/Medicaid claims, etc.) are accessible only through the **NCHS Research Data Center (RDC)** for a fee, via proposals submitted through the federal **Standard Application Process portal** (researchdatagov.org). Public-use "feasibility files" let researchers assess linkage sample sizes before applying.

**Harmonized/preserved versions:**
- **IPUMS NHIS** (University of Minnesota Population Center) is the major third-party harmonization project: 60+ years of data (1963–present), 17,000+ integrated variables with consistent names/codes, crosswalks to original NCHS variables, linking keys (NHISHID/NHISPID), documentation of comparability breaks (including the 2019 redesign), an online tabulator, and free custom extracts. Indispensable for cross-time research and a de facto preservation layer.
- NCHS also publishes analyses through *National Health Statistic Reports*, the **Early Release Program** (preliminary quarterly/biannual estimates on timely topics like health insurance and wireless phone substitution, released months ahead of full public-use files), and interactive **data query tools/dashboards**.

## 6. Users and Uses (for the policy activist)

- **Federal government:** NHIS is the source of the official national estimates of the uninsured and health coverage (used by HHS/ASPE, CBO, CMS to monitor ACA effects and the 2023–24 Medicaid "unwinding"); a designated data source for **Healthy People national objectives**; used throughout HHS to track illness/disability trends, evaluate federal programs, and set research priorities. Other agencies sponsor content (food security, cancer screening, etc.).
- **Researchers:** one of the most heavily used datasets in health services research, epidemiology, and social science — thousands of peer-reviewed papers on disparities, disability, smoking, access to care, and mortality follow-up.
- **State and local users, think tanks, journalists:** subgroup estimates by age, race/ethnicity, geography, income, and employment (a stated core strength, given the large sample); state-level estimates are produced for some measures (e.g., wireless substitution).
- **Policy relevance examples:** quarterly uninsured estimates during the COVID-19 public health emergency and Medicaid unwinding; wireless-substitution estimates used to adjust telephone-survey methodology government-wide; disability and functional-status measures informing benefit policy.

## 7. Public Benefits

NCHS frames NHIS as the mechanism by which the nation tracks the health status of its people, their access to care, and progress toward national health goals — data that "drive policies and programs to improve health." Its distinguishing public values are: (1) **universality and representativeness** (household-based, so it captures people missed by medical-records-based surveys); (2) **longevity** — nearly 70 years of continuous trend data; (3) **free, open microdata** with strong confidentiality protections; (4) **disaggregation** — reliable estimates for population subgroups; and (5) **timeliness mechanisms** like the Early Release Program.

## 8. Caveats an honest report should include

- Excludes institutionalized and active-duty populations (undercounts the sickest populations).
- Response rates near 45–48% raise nonresponse concerns; NCHS mitigates via paradata-based weighting, but 2020 especially should be used with caution.
- The 2019 redesign creates a comparability break with 1997–2018; the 1997 redesign similarly broke trends with 1982–1996.
- Face-to-face household interviewing is being supplemented/tested with web and paper modes (part of the 2028 redesign), which will eventually be another methodological transition to document.
